summary:
Jeremiah son of Hilkiah came from a family of priests in Anathoth, a village a few miles northeast of Jerusalem. God's word came to him in the thirteenth year of King Josiah (1:2), about 627 BC, and kept coming for some forty years, under Judah's last five kings, until Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC. He protested — "I am only a child" (1:6) — and was answered: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart" (1:5). His commission: "to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant" (1:10). A first vision turns on a pun: an almond branch — Hebrew shaqed, echoing shoqed, "watching" — because "I am watching over My word to accomplish it" (1:12).

His message stayed constant: Judah had broken its covenant (its formal bond with God) by serving other gods, and Babylon was coming as God's judgment. In the temple sermon he attacked the worshipers' chant of safety, "This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD" (7:4), and asked, "Has this house, which bears My Name, become a den of robbers in your sight?" (7:11) — the words Jesus takes up when he clears the temple (Matthew 21:13). Priests and prophets seized him for it, shouting "You must surely die!" (26:8); elders saved him by recalling that Micah had preached "Zion will be plowed like a field" under Hezekiah and gone unpunished (26:18, quoting Micah 3:12).

Personal laments, often called Jeremiah's "confessions" (chapters 11–20), record what the calling cost: "Cursed be the day I was born!" (20:14). When he resolves to stop speaking, the message becomes "a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones" (20:9). His tears — "Oh, that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears!" (9:1; 13:17) — are behind his traditional label, "the weeping prophet." He was beaten and locked in stocks (20:2), and during the final siege was dropped into a muddy cistern to die (38:6–13). Other signs were acted out: the potter reworking a flawed vessel (18) and a wooden yoke urging surrender to Babylon; when the prophet Hananiah broke it, the reply was "a yoke of iron," and Hananiah died that year (28:13–17).

The exile, he announced, would last seventy years (25:11; 29:10), the figure Daniel later reads (Daniel 9:2). To the deportees in Babylon he wrote: "Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles" (29:7); "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope" (29:11). Chapters 30–33, often called the Book of Consolation, announce "a new covenant" (31:31) — the phrase's only appearance in the Old Testament, and the phrase behind the name "New Testament": "I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts" (31:33). Jesus takes it up at the Last Supper ("the new covenant in My blood," Luke 22:20), and Hebrews 8:8–12 quotes the passage in full. During the siege Jeremiah bought his cousin's field at Anathoth and sealed the deed in a clay jar: "Houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in this land" (32:15).

Chapter 36 shows the book being made: Jeremiah dictated his oracles to the scribe Baruch (a professional document-writer); King Jehoiakim sliced the scroll apart three or four columns at a time and burned it, and a second dictation added "many similar words" (36:32). The book, usually reckoned the Bible's longest by Hebrew word count, survives in two forms: the ancient Greek translation is roughly one-eighth shorter and places the oracles against the nations (chapters 46–51) mid-book rather than at the end — evidence, many scholars conclude, of two early editions. After Jerusalem fell (chapters 39 and 52), survivors fleeing to Egypt took Jeremiah along against his will (43:5–7); later tradition says he died there. The oracles close with "Here end the words of Jeremiah" (51:64), and chapter 52, an appendix matching the end of 2 Kings (24:18–25:30), gives the final scene: after thirty-seven years, Judah's exiled king Jehoiachin is released from prison and "dined regularly at the king's table for the rest of his life" (52:31–34).
